findings.title: Deny-cache test does not show the denial cache is what denies
findings.body: The comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but the permCache entry is `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`. `checkPermission` reads `scopeMap[t.scope(req.Name)]` (service.go:558), so a `false` value is a deny. The request also carries `Folder: "fold1"`, which sends a miss into `checkInheritedPermissions` and `buildFolderTree` (service.go:581-590). The assertion `Allowed == false` can therefore hold without the denial-cache short-circuit ever running, or the test fails for an unrelated reason. Set the value to `true`, so the result can only be a deny if `permDenialCache` is read before `permCache`. The test also never checks that a denied `Check` writes the denial entry (service.go:153-155). Add a case for that: run a denied Check, then assert `permDenialCache.Get` hits.

findings.title: Denial cache key is ambiguous and shares the `perm_` prefix with permission keys
findings.body: `ns.perm_<uid>_<action>_<name>_<parent>` joins free-form fields with `_`, and folder and dashboard UIDs may contain `_`. For example, name=`a` with parent=`b_` and name=`a_b` with parent=`` both give `..._a_b_`, so a denial for one resource can deny a different one for up to 30s. The key also starts with `perm_<uid>_<action>`, the same prefix as `userPermCacheKey`, and both caches share one backing `cache.Cache`. A distinct prefix (`ns.perm_denial_...`) and a separator that cannot occur in UIDs would remove both problems. The failure is fail-closed and the cache lives only 30s, so this is a judgement call.

findings.title: `cacheHit` in TestService_getUserPermissions is now always false
findings.body: The cache-hit case was removed because `getUserPermissions` no longer reads `permCache`. The `cacheHit` field, the `if tc.cacheHit` Set (line 367) and the `store.calls` branch (line 389) are now dead. Remove them so the table does not suggest a cache path that no longer exists in this function.

findings.title: Exported NoopCache in package authz
findings.body: `NoopCache` is only used in this file, for the in-process client, but it is exported and gets a public API in `authz`. Unexport it (`noopCache`), or check whether authlib already provides a no-op cache option. Also add a comment saying why the in-proc client skips its own cache: the server now caches, and a client-side TTL would stack on top of it.

contracts.action: Check consults a per-(user, action, name, folder) denial cache, then the permission cache, and falls back to the DB when cached permissions do not allow
contracts.equivalent_path: The previous flow in `getUserPermissions` and `getAnonymousPermissions` returned the cached scope map from `permCache` and used it for the decision, even when it was stale. Both functions are called from `getIdentityPermissions`.
contracts.before_after: Before, a cached scope map was authoritative: a stale map that lacked a scope gave a deny for the whole TTL. Now a cached allow returns early, a cached non-allow falls through to the DB (service.go:139), and a DB deny writes the denial entry (service.go:153-155). The DB path still writes `permCache` (service.go:406, 430).
contracts.visible_effect: Fewer DB reads for repeated allowed and denied checks. A grant becomes visible on the next non-denied Check. A denial entry persists for up to shortCacheTTL (30s, service.go:32), so a freshly granted permission can still be denied for that long on the same resource.
contracts.failure_mode: If `getCachedIdentityPermissions` fails (e.g. `GetUserIdentifiers` errors), the error is swallowed. `getIdentityPermissions` then repeats the lookup and reports the error, so the failing call runs twice. Cache Get and Set errors are only logged by `cacheWrap`, never returned, so a cache outage degrades to DB reads.

contracts.action: The in-process authz client is built with a NoopCache instead of the 30s local cache; the remote client keeps the local cache
contracts.before_after: Before, both modes used `newRBACClient` with the 30s local cache. Now the in-proc client always calls the in-process server, which caches itself (service.go), and the remote client keeps client-side caching.
contracts.visible_effect: A change in permissions shows up sooner on the in-proc path (at most the server's 30s TTL, with no extra client-side TTL).
contracts.failure_mode: None found. NoopCache.Get returns `cache.ErrNotFound`, which is the miss signal the cacheWrap code also uses (cache.go:64).

summary: The caching change is logically sound: cached allows return early, cached non-allows fall back to the DB, and DB denies are cached for 30s. I found one test that does not show what its comment claims (the explicit deny-entry test), one dead test field, an ambiguous denial-cache key format, and an exported NoopCache that could be unexported. I did not build or run anything.
